newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. official positive on HK but warns on rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official positive on HK but warns on rights.

text.p: A top U.S. Treasury official heaped praise on Hong Kong's financial system as the territory prepares for its reversion to China, but he warned that politics as well as economics were key elements of prosperity.

U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Monday the United States welcomed the decision by Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, to retain the top tier of the civil service in his post-handover administration.

"Mr Tung's recent decision to leave current (policy secretaries) in their posts, including Hong Kong's extremely competent economic team, is very reassuring," Summers told a luncheon meeting of the American Chamber of Commerce.
"It adds weight to the reassurances that have been given at the highest political levels that Hong Kong's sound financial and economic system will remain intact," he said.
Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule.

Last month, Tung, chosen in December to be Hong Kong's first Chief Executive, announced that 21 of the 23 top civil servants would stay in their posts following the handover, including Financial Secretary Donald Tsang and Secretary for Financial Services Rafael Hui.
The current Attorney-General, a Briton, does not meet the nationality requirements to serve after 1997. The head of Hong Kong's anti-corruption squad had earlier announced his plans to retire.
Summers said the transition presents a tremendous opportunity for China to take even greater advantage of Hong Kong's capital and technological resources to further advance the mainland's economy.
But he repeated in blunt terms the U.S. view that the economic prosperity of both Hong Kong and China will be at risk if China fails to maintain Hong Kong's freedoms.
China's plans to roll back some of Hong Kong's key civil liberties laws has angered Britain, its allies and Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy movement.
China maintains the revisions will be technical and will not materially affect the freedoms Hong Kong people now take for granted.

"The free flow of information is essential to a free society, to free markets, and to a strong financial system. It is essential to Hong Kong's prosperity, and to China's, that information flow freely," Summers said.

He said that even a perceived risk that China was seeking to undermine Hong Kong's autonomy could "severely damage Hong Kong's standing in international financial circles and, by association, its economic prospects".
Hong Kong people could make such a blunder extremely costly for China, either by leaving the territory outright or by transferring their funds elsewhere, he said.
"This would not only be disastrous for the Hong Kong economy, but the loss to China would be immense," he said.
Summers was in Hong Kong for a one-day visit before travelling to Tokyo to meet with officials from Japan, China, Singapore, Australia and Hong Kong for the "Six Markets Meeting".
He said he had spoken with Financial Secretary Tsang while in the territory and had a meeting planned with Tung.
